PART I
ITEM 1. BUSINESS

nodes.title: ABOUT PFIZER
nodes.summary: Pfizer is a global, research-based biopharmaceutical company incorporated in Delaware in 1942, focused on discovering, developing, manufacturing and distributing therapies worldwide and expanding access to affordable healthcare. Most revenue comes from medicines and vaccines, whose value, pricing and payer arrangements are evaluated to improve outcomes and patient access. Its purpose is to change patients’ lives, guided by five strategic “Bold Moves” and six ESG priorities. Growth relies on pipeline advances, existing products and business development; notable 2021 collaborations and acquisitions included Arvinas, Biohaven, Trillium, Beam and the proposed Arena acquisition. COVID-19 affected operations and finances in 2020–21; Pfizer developed a vaccine and oral treatment.

nodes.title: COMMERCIAL OPERATIONS
nodes.summary: After spinning off Upjohn into Viatris and forming the GSK Consumer Healthcare JV, Pfizer operated as one segment from late 2020, then reorganized in fiscal Q4 2021 into Biopharma and PC1 (contract development/manufacturing and specialty APIs). The text outlines Biopharma’s six therapeutic areas—Vaccines, Oncology, Internal Medicine, Hospital, Inflammation & Immunology, and Rare Disease—their scope and key products. It identifies products with specified billion-dollar revenues, explains alliance/direct-sales and Prevnar-family coverage, notes PC1’s prior Hospital classification and Meridian’s 2021 sale, and points to segment, revenue-driver, and product-concentration disclosures.

nodes.title: COLLABORATION AND CO-PROMOTION
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes collaborations and co-promotion arrangements supporting development, R&D, sales and distribution. Comirnaty is jointly developed and commercialized with BioNTech, with equal development costs and gross profits, subject to market approvals and territorial exclusions; most revenue is recorded as direct product revenue. Eliquis is jointly developed and commercialized with BMS, with shared costs and profits, subject to market-specific terms. Xtandi’s U.S. profits, losses and costs are shared equally with Astellas, while international sales generate tiered royalties. Bavencio development and commercialization costs and profits are largely shared equally with Merck KGaA. Orgovyx and Myfembree are developed with Myovant, with U.S. and Canadian profits and allowable expenses shared equally; Myovant covers Pfizer’s expenses up to $50 million in 2022 and leads regulatory matters, supply and combination-tablet development. Other collaboration revenue is generally reported as Alliance revenue, with exceptions for direct sales. Pipeline collaborations include BioNTech’s shingles vaccine and Valneva’s Lyme disease vaccine VLA15. The text refers readers to related risk factors and financial-statement notes.

nodes.title: RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
key_items: Our R&D Priorities and Strategy; Our R&D Operations
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes R&D priorities, strategy, external collaborations, global research and clinical-development platforms, portfolio governance, expense reporting, pipeline timelines and risks. It outlines international reach, emerging-market opportunities, overseas revenues and country rankings, alongside global operating risks. It also explains sales channels for medicines and vaccines, government contracts, formulary and payer engagement, and promotion to healthcare professionals, patients, insurers, employers and agencies, including direct-to-consumer and public-health advertising.

nodes.title: R&D, International Operations, Sales and Marketing
nodes.summary: Drug and biological product development can take over ten years; candidates and supplemental filings are discussed elsewhere, and R&D risks are identified in the Form 10-K. Pfizer sells in over 125 countries, with emerging markets offering growth opportunities; international sales were $51.5 billion, or 63% of 2021 revenue, and Japan was its largest non-U.S. market. Global operations carry country-specific risks. Products are sold mainly through wholesalers and institutional and government customers; committed Comirnaty and Paxlovid contracts contributed significantly to 2021 revenue. Pfizer seeks formulary access, works with payers on disease-management programs, and promotes products and public health through provider, patient, consumer, and general advertising.

nodes.title: PATENTS AND OTHER INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS
key_items: Japan Basic Product Patent Expiration Year (1)
nodes.summary: Pfizer owns or licenses patents covering products, uses, formulations and manufacturing, with protection varying by country, patent terms, claims and remedies; some jurisdictions offer patent-term extensions and drug regulatory exclusivity, while weak IP protection can limit operations. A table lists major products’ basic patent expirations across the U.S., Europe and Japan, with qualifications on extensions, exclusivity, pending approvals and product-specific patent status. Notes explain expiry rules and details on Chantix, Sutent, Prevenar 13, Eliquis litigation and generic launch scenarios, collaboration and commercialization rights, royalties, and Comirnaty and Paxlovid patent applications. Patent loss, expiry, invalidation, settlements or lost licensing rights may trigger lower-priced generic or biosimilar competition and materially reduce revenue; Pfizer defends its rights, expects further competition for some products, and refers readers to risk disclosures and financial analysis. Trademarks and trade dress protect branded products through renewable registrations or use-based protection, and are important to Pfizer.

nodes.title: COMPETITION
nodes.summary: The text describes intense competition in regulated markets from branded, generic and biosimilar medicines, assessed on efficacy, safety, convenience and cost. Competitors’ R&D and patent challenges can erode sales or make products obsolete. The company responds with substantial R&D and business development, post-approval research, stakeholder education, ethical marketing, organizational improvements and affordability/access programs. Vaccines face alternative and next-generation products; biosimilars compete with biologics and seek early market entry. Generics benefit from lower costs, simplified approvals, substitution policies and payer and government preferences, with intensified competition expected in China. Biosimilars are highly similar, lower-cost biologics approved under U.S. law.

nodes.title: PRICING PRESSURES AND MANAGED CARE ORGANIZATIONS
nodes.summary: The text describes commercial pricing pressures from cost-focused employers, payers and provider purchasing groups, plus a shift toward outcomes-based and risk-sharing payments that may lower prices or restrict access but encourage preventive drug use. COVID-19 may weaken participation in downside-risk models while supporting capitation. The company advocates affordability and access, engages payers, government and health-value bodies, and builds capabilities to demonstrate product value. It also explains MCOs’ growing, consolidated influence; their use of formularies, protocols, purchasing and cost-sharing to control spending; ACA-driven outcome-based reimbursement; coverage variation and preference for preventive or cost-saving treatments; and the effects of formulary exclusion or tier placement. The company reports broad, though not universal, coverage, with more branded products becoming non-preferred.

nodes.title: RAW MATERIALS
nodes.summary: The company sources essential raw materials from numerous global suppliers, generally in sufficient quantities and often from multiple sources. It anticipates no significant availability-related operational impact in 2022, but rising industry demand for certain components and materials may constrain supply and affect future business. It is monitoring risks and mitigating them through supplier management, qualifying additional suppliers, and advance purchasing where possible.

nodes.title: GOVERNMENT REGULATION AND PRICE CONSTRAINTS
key_items: Drug and Biologic Regulation; Biosimilar Regulation
Pricing, Reimbursement and Access Regulations; Anti-Corruption; Data Privacy
Healthcare Provider Transparency and Disclosures; Intellectual Property; Data Privacy
nodes.summary: The text outlines extensive global regulation of Pfizer’s biopharmaceutical operations, associated compliance costs and potential penalties, while noting no currently expected material effect on capital spending or competitiveness. In the U.S., it covers FDA and other-agency oversight of drug development, approval, manufacturing, safety, promotion, supply chains and emergency authorizations; biosimilar exclusivity; fraud, marketing, anti-corruption and privacy rules; and pricing, reimbursement, rebates, Medicaid/340B, payer and state cost-control pressures. International topics include approval and safety authorities, government pricing and access controls, China’s reimbursement and generic-tender systems, provider-payment disclosures, uneven intellectual-property protections and advocacy, and evolving privacy laws.

nodes.title: ENVIRONMENTAL MATTERS
nodes.summary: The company complies with environmental laws, budgets for ongoing compliance, and is cleaning up contamination from past industrial activity. In 2021, it spent $55 million on environmental capital projects and $152 million on other environmental expenses. It does not expect environmental costs to materially affect capital spending or competitiveness. Climate risks include regulation and costs, severe weather, and water shortages affecting its facilities and suppliers; it reviews these risks and currently considers them non-material, though future impacts cannot be ruled out.

nodes.title: HUMAN CAPITAL
key_items: Core Values; Diversity, Equity and Inclusion; Colleague Engagement; Performance, Leadership and Growth; Health, Safety and Well-Being; Pay Equity
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes its 2021 workforce, diversity and efforts to attract, retain and support employees through inclusive practices, career mobility, and competitive compensation and benefits. Its values are Courage, Excellence, Equity and Joy. Diversity initiatives address representation, inclusion, equitable health outcomes, allyship, external partnerships and representative clinical trials. Employee engagement is measured through the Pfizer Pulse survey; 90% reported engagement and 92% saw a connection between daily work and Pfizer’s purpose. Performance and development programs provide six-month feedback cycles, growth frameworks, mentoring, rotations and learning. Health and safety efforts include EHS risk management, COVID-19 protections, vaccination, and mental-health and wellness resources. Pfizer also commits to role-based equitable pay and annual public pay-equity reporting.

nodes.title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS
nodes.summary: Pfizer warns that its listed risks are not exhaustive, alongside general economic, geopolitical and natural-disaster risks, and that materialized uncertainties could harm operations, finances, cash flow, prospects, reputation or credit ratings. Managed-care consolidation, formularies, cost controls, generic substitution, specialty-drug costs and regulatory scrutiny may limit pricing and access. Competitor launches, generics, patent challenges, at-risk launches and biosimilars threaten sales; Pfizer’s own biosimilars face pricing and uptake barriers. Revenue is concentrated: nine products generated 75% of 2021 revenue, including Comirnaty/BNT162b2 at 45%, exposing results to product, safety, regulatory, competitive, access, supply and exclusivity setbacks.

nodes.title: Business Risks, Managed Care and Competition
key_items: RISKS RELATED TO OUR BUSINESS, INDUSTRY AND OPERATIONS:
nodes.summary: The page notes that its risk discussion is not exhaustive and that general risks, including economic, geopolitical and natural events, could materially harm operations, finances, prospects, reputation or credit ratings; risk factors include forward-looking statements. Managed-care consolidation, formularies, cost controls, utilization restrictions, generic substitution, specialty-drug costs and regulatory scrutiny may constrain product access, pricing and placement. Competition—from new products, generics (including at-risk launches), biosimilars and generic challenges to partners’ patents—may erode sales, cause obsolescence, price cuts or lost volume; biosimilar uptake may also be limited by access, prescribing and incentive barriers.

nodes.title: CONCENTRATION
nodes.summary: Nine products generated over $1 billion each and together represented 75% of Pfizer’s 2021 revenue; Comirnaty/BNT162b2 alone contributed 45%. Revenue could be harmed by patent or exclusivity losses, slower prescription or vaccination growth, liability claims, safety or regulatory issues, negative publicity, competition, labeling or pricing pressures, access restrictions, supply shortages, or superior new products. Some products have faced exclusivity expirations, and patents on bestsellers are under legal challenge. Comirnaty and Paxlovid may earn less after the pandemic. Pfizer also faces risks from financial difficulties at major U.S. wholesalers, delayed or uncollected payments, and growing competitive and pricing pressures from wholesaler and pharmacy-chain consolidation.

nodes.title: RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
nodes.summary: Continued business strength and growth depend on replenishing product lines through internal R&D and external partnerships, developing products or new indications for unmet needs, and securing payer reimbursement. High development costs and regulatory demands constrain investment, while balancing current growth, future investment, and shareholder returns is challenging. Early development choices affect marketing and reimbursement; trials may not achieve the right balance of speed and outcomes, and candidates can fail or lack approval. Poor indication selection or resource allocation, unsuccessful science, competitive pressures, and access barriers can reduce pipeline productivity. Novel gene therapies carry especially uncertain development timelines, costs, approval prospects, and acceptance by patients and clinicians.

nodes.title: GLOBAL OPERATIONS
nodes.summary: Pfizer outlines risks from global operations, including geopolitical and economic instability, trade barriers, government price controls, emerging-market uncertainty, inflation, and currency and interest-rate exposure; it is preparing for the LIBOR-to-SOFR transition. Manufacturing, supply, distribution, and sales may be disrupted by regulatory issues, recalls, shortages, disasters, or contractor failures. Chantix was recalled globally following nitrosamine findings, and broader industry testing may prompt further actions. Third-party collaborators and service providers can delay or impair development and commercialization, while expiring alliances may reduce revenue. Counterfeit medicines threaten patient safety, reputation, and sales, particularly through online channels; Pfizer’s mitigation efforts may not fully succeed.

nodes.title: Operational, Partnership, and Counterfeit Product Risks
key_items: PRODUCT MANUFACTURING, SALES AND MARKETING RISKS
COLLABORATIONS AND OTHER RELATIONSHIPS WITH THIRD PARTIES
nodes.summary: Pfizer expects the LIBOR-to-SOFR transition to have no significant business or financial impact. Manufacturing, supply, distribution, sales, and marketing may be disrupted by operational, regulatory, quality, or external events; inspections and noncompliance can trigger penalties or halt production. Chantix was recalled and shipments paused due to nitrosamine, with solutions under development and further product actions possible. Third-party collaborators and service providers support Pfizer’s operations, but failures, disruptions, upfront transaction costs, or expiring agreements may harm results and product development. Counterfeits threaten patient safety, trust, and sales, especially online and for COVID-19 products; mitigation efforts may not prevent their growth.

summary: Part I describes Pfizer’s business, strategy, products, therapeutic areas, collaborations, R&D, international operations, sales and marketing, intellectual property, competition, pricing and managed care, raw materials, regulation, environmental responsibilities, and human capital. It also outlines risk factors, including pricing and access constraints, product and revenue concentration, patent loss and competition, R&D uncertainty, global and operational disruptions, reliance on partners and suppliers, and counterfeit medicines.

title: RISKS RELATED TO GOVERNMENT REGULATION AND LEGAL PROCEEDINGS:
key_items: PRICING AND REIMBURSEMENT; U.S. HEALTHCARE REGULATION
DEVELOPMENT, REGULATORY APPROVAL AND MARKETING OF PRODUCTS
summary: Pfizer faces global pricing and reimbursement pressures from government controls, tenders, healthcare reforms, budget cuts and COVID-19-related fiscal pressures, which may restrict access or reduce revenue. Drug development and approval are lengthy, costly and uncertain; regulators’ decisions, trial outcomes, safety concerns, advisory recommendations and post-approval data can delay, limit or remove approvals and damage sales. The text details post-marketing requirements and Xeljanz, Comirnaty and Paxlovid examples. Legal risks include patent, product, commercial, regulatory and other litigation; investigations, compliance enforcement, fines, reputational harm, CIA obligations, and uncertain legal and environmental liabilities.

title: RISKS RELATED TO INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY, TECHNOLOGY AND SECURITY:
summary: The text describes risks to Pfizer’s intellectual property and technology. Patent, trademark, trade-secret and licensing protections may be unavailable, delayed, limited, challenged, weakened by national laws or policy changes, or difficult to enforce, enabling imitation and generic or biosimilar competition; disputes can involve invalidity, infringement, antitrust, damages, regulatory challenges and at-risk launches. Third-party patent claims may delay or block products or result in royalties, damages or lost sales, while biosimilar opportunities may fail. Cyberattacks, system outages and security weaknesses involving Pfizer, vendors or partners could expose confidential information, disrupt operations and cause financial, legal or reputational harm; insurance may not cover resulting losses.

title: RISKS RELATED TO BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT:
key_items: BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT ACTIVITIES; SPIN-OFF AND COMBINATION OF UPJOHN WITH MYLAN
SPIN-OFF AND COMBINATION OF UPJOHN WITH MYLAN
summary: The text outlines risks from business development, including difficulty identifying and completing deals, financing needs, investment-value declines, limited control, undiscovered liabilities, integration failures, employee or relationship disruption, and missed savings, growth or product revenue due to clinical, regulatory or commercialization setbacks. It also warns that Pfizer may not achieve benefits from the Upjohn–Mylan combination and that transition services may divert resources. As a minority owner of the GSK consumer-health JV, Pfizer depends on GSK’s management; the proposed demerger, any public listing, and future stake sales face timing, market and execution uncertainty that could harm the JV and Pfizer’s results.

It also covers volatility in investment values and benefit obligations, cost-control and unusual-event risks, impairment risks for intangible assets, goodwill and equity investments, and adverse effects of legal or accounting changes. It describes Pfizer’s global properties, headquarters relocation, manufacturing and distribution footprint, and property adequacy; refers to legal proceedings in Note 16A; and lists four executive officers’ ages, roles and career histories.

It describes the company’s global properties, headquarters relocation plans, PGS leadership locations, plants and distribution facilities, and states that its properties are adequate for foreseeable operations. Legal proceedings are discussed in Note 16A.

title: ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

nodes.title: OVERVIEW OF OUR PERFORMANCE, OPERATING ENVIRONMENT, STRATEGY AND OUTLOOK
Financial Highlights
nodes.summary: The section presents 2021 financial highlights: revenue of $81.3 billion, operating cash flow of $32.6 billion, reported diluted EPS of $3.85, and adjusted diluted EPS (non-GAAP) of $4.42. These increased 95%, 126%, 137%, and 96%, respectively, from 2020. It directs readers to the MD&A for adjusted EPS reconciliations and explains that operational variances exclude foreign-exchange effects to clarify business trends, since exchange rates are outside the company’s control.

nodes.title: Our Business and Strategy
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s revenues primarily come from biopharmaceutical products. Following the Consumer Healthcare JV formation and Upjohn spin-off, it reorganized from one operating segment to Biopharma and PC1, with Biopharma the sole reportable segment; Meridian, Upjohn, and the Mylan-Japan collaboration are treated as discontinued operations, and prior periods were restated. Upjohn separation costs are expected to total about $700 million, roughly 75% incurred by year-end 2021. Pfizer is aligning costs, corporate support, and commercial engagement with its new structure. Its R&D strategy aims to advance and improve medicines, drawing on its pipeline and growth opportunities from aging populations, scientific and digital advances, and hospitals’ growing healthcare role.

nodes.title: Our Business Development Initiatives
nodes.summary: The company pursues growth by advancing its product pipeline, maximizing existing products, and reviewing its portfolio and business development opportunities. Recent initiatives include a proposed $6.7 billion all-cash acquisition of clinical-stage Arena, approved by Arena shareholders and targeted to close in the first half of 2022 pending regulatory and customary conditions; and a completed Biohaven agreement granting exclusive rights to commercialize migraine treatments rimegepant and zavegepant outside the U.S. Biohaven leads global R&D. The company paid $500 million at closing and may owe up to $740 million in milestones, tiered double-digit royalties, and certain third-party payments. Further details are referenced in Note 2.

nodes.title: Our 2021 Performance
key_items: Income from Continuing Operations Before Provision/(Benefit) for Taxes on Income
nodes.summary: In 2021, Pfizer revenue rose $39.6 billion (95%) to $81.3 billion, driven by $38.4 billion in operational growth and $1.2 billion from foreign exchange. Excluding Comirnaty direct and alliance sales and Paxlovid sales, operational revenue grew 6%, led by several products and therapeutic areas, partly offset by declines in others. Pretax income from continuing operations increased $17.3 billion, mainly due to higher revenue, benefit credits, lower impairment charges and higher equity-security gains, partly offset by increased operating expenses. The text directs readers to MD&A and notes for revenue, product, tax and effective-tax-rate details.

nodes.title: Our Operating Environment
key_items: Intellectual Property Rights and Collaboration/Licensing Rights
Regulatory Environment/Pricing and Access––Government and Other Payer Group Pressures
nodes.summary: The text outlines industry challenges: costly, risky R&D and clinical development needed to replenish products, plus ongoing safety monitoring that can lead to regulatory action and reduced sales. Patent loss, litigation settlements, and expiring collaboration or licensing rights may reduce revenue, though patent-related impacts are expected to be moderate through 2025; the company defends its rights. Government and payer efforts to control medicine costs—including discounts, formularies, price reforms, Medicare negotiation proposals, inflation penalties, and Medicaid/340B changes—create global pricing pressure. Supply delays, disruptions, shortages, and recalls, including Chantix, are also noted.

nodes.title: The Global Economic Environment
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s global operations are exposed to economic cycles and risks including currency fluctuations, capital and exchange controls, inflation and other economic conditions, restrictive government actions, changes in intellectual-property protections, trade and tax rules, and policies affecting product approval, production, pricing, marketing, reimbursement, and access. Further risks include political or civil unrest, military conflict (including Russia-Ukraine), terrorism, unstable governments and legal systems, intergovernmental disputes, public-health outbreaks, epidemics, pandemics, natural disasters, and climate-related disruptions. Government involvement in pricing, access criteria, and cost controls can also create negative pricing pressure.

nodes.title: COVID-19 Pandemic
key_items: • IV Protease Inhibitor:; Impact of COVID-19 on Our Business and Operations
Impact of COVID-19 on Our Business and Operations
nodes.summary: COVID-19 affected Pfizer’s business, operations, and financial results. Pfizer describes its pandemic response and its collaboration with BioNTech on Comirnaty, including U.S. and international authorizations, ongoing efficacy and variant studies, manufacturing and global supply plans, access for lower-income countries, and projected 2022 revenue. It covers Paxlovid’s emergency authorization, trials in additional populations, supply agreements, generic licensing, production targets, and projected revenue. Pfizer also discontinued development of its IV protease inhibitor and notes that operational and financial planning relies on assumptions about the pandemic’s duration, severity, and macroeconomic effects.

nodes.title: Pfizer Inc.
nodes.summary: Pfizer cannot predict the pandemic’s full effects, including on COVID-19 vaccine and treatment supply, and is using digital tools and other measures to mitigate risks. Product impacts varied: COVID-related healthcare disruptions affected some vaccines and procedures, while demand for Ibrance recovered. Healthcare-professional engagement shifted to hybrid formats; remote work, onsite safety protocols, and high U.S. employee vaccination rates continued. Manufacturing and supply chains remained largely stable, though component shortages pose risks; clinical trials faced recruitment and supply challenges but used decentralized methods. Pfizer will monitor developments and warns significant disruption or reduced demand could materially harm its business and results; it refers readers to its COVID-19 risk factors.

The section reviews Pfizer’s 2021 financial highlights and performance, business structure, strategy, R&D priorities and business-development deals. It describes industry and global economic challenges, including development risks, patent and pricing pressures, supply disruptions, and geopolitical, regulatory, public-health and climate risks. It details COVID-19’s effects and Pfizer’s response—including Comirnaty and Paxlovid development, authorizations, supply, access and revenue plans—along with operational impacts, mitigation measures, uncertainties and potential material risks.

nodes.title: SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES AND APPLICATION OF CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES AND ASSUMPTIONS

It explains acquisition fair-value accounting; revenue deductions and estimation uncertainty, especially delayed U.S. government and performance-based rebates; impairment indicators and valuation methods for identifiable intangibles and goodwill, noting no goodwill impairment in 2021; and benefit-plan assumptions, historical returns, discount rates, and sensitivities. It also describes income-tax assets and uncertain tax positions, plus ordinary-course tax, legal, guarantee, and indemnification contingencies.

nodes.summary: The text reports Pfizer’s 2019–2021 revenues by operating segment and geography, with annual comparisons and percentage changes. It explains 2021 growth drivers and declines by geography, including Comirnaty, other products, manufacturing, foreign exchange, and emerging-market growth; and 2020 changes, including product performance, the Consumer Healthcare joint-venture exit, COVID-19 effects, currency impacts, and emerging markets. It also describes estimated gross-revenue deductions, their drivers and estimation, and lists 2019–2021 amounts for rebates, chargebacks, allowances, returns, and discounts, referencing Note 1H for accrual details.

nodes.title: Revenue Deductions
nodes.summary: The text analyzes Pfizer’s 2020 revenue changes versus 2019 worldwide, in the U.S. and internationally, citing product and market growth, the Consumer Healthcare joint-venture transaction, declines in Enbrel and Chantix/Champix, other operational factors and foreign exchange. It describes an estimated $700 million COVID-19 revenue impact and emerging-market results. It explains revenue deductions, their estimation and drivers, provides deduction totals for 2019–2021, and references Note 1H. Finally, it presents 2021 global and regional revenues and year-over-year growth for selected Biopharma products, including Comirnaty, Eliquis, Ibrance, Prevnar, Xeljanz, Vyndaqel/Vyndamax, Xtandi and Inlyta.

nodes.title: Operational Results Commentary
nodes.summary: The text reviews 2021 product and business-unit revenue performance, reporting growth, flat results, or declines and explaining key drivers: market adoption and launches, indication and regional trends, COVID-19 disruptions, pricing and channel mix, patient-assistance use, and regulatory or safety developments. It includes revenue figures and year-over-year changes for biosimilars, hospital products, and Pfizer CentreOne, plus a Comirnaty revenue and manufacturing footnote and references to patent, litigation, and product-indication disclosures. It then presents 2019–2021 costs and expenses and explains the 2021 cost-of-sales increase, with a partial discussion of 2020 drivers.

nodes.title: Pfizer CentreOne Revenue and Costs
nodes.summary: Reports Pfizer CentreOne and related 2021 revenue by product and region, year-over-year changes, and commentary attributing growth to biosimilar launches, Retacrit, anti-infectives, and manufacturing for Viatris and BioNTech. Clarifies Comirnaty revenue treatment and PC1 manufacturing revenues, and points to patent, litigation, and product-indication disclosures. Provides 2019–2021 costs and expenses, then explains cost-of-sales increases in 2021 versus 2020 and 2020 versus 2019, including vaccine profit-sharing and royalties, sales volumes, foreign exchange, alliance revenue, and pandemic-related costs.

nodes.title: Costs and Expenses
key_items: Selling, Informational and Administrative (SI&A) Expenses; Research and Development (R&D) Expenses; Amortization of Intangible Assets
Restructuring Charges and Other Costs Associated with Acquisitions and Cost-Reduction/Productivity Initiatives
Other (Income)/Deductions––Net; Provision/(Benefit) for Taxes on Income; Discontinued Operations
nodes.summary: The excerpt reports 2021 and comparative 2020 revenues by region and operating segment, highlighting biosimilar, hospital, Pfizer CentreOne and anti-infective growth drivers, and explains Comirnaty revenue classification and PC1 manufacturing revenue. It summarizes costs and expenses and year-over-year causes for changes in cost of sales, selling and administrative, R&D, intangible amortization, restructuring and other income/deductions. It outlines expected savings from Pfizer’s transformation program, refers to relevant notes on patents, litigation and products, presents income-tax provisions and effective rates, and directs readers to disclosures on taxes and discontinued operations.

Analyzes Pfizer’s 2019–2021 revenues by segment, geography, and selected products, explaining annual growth and declines through product performance, Comirnaty, market adoption, COVID-19 effects, manufacturing, foreign exchange, pricing, and the Consumer Healthcare joint-venture exit. Details estimated revenue deductions, their drivers and amounts. Reviews 2021 operational results, including biosimilars, hospital products, and Pfizer CentreOne, with product and regional drivers and relevant patent, litigation, and indication disclosures. Presents costs and expenses and explains year-over-year changes across cost of sales, selling and administrative, R&D, amortization, restructuring, and other income or deductions; also covers transformation savings, income taxes, effective rates, and related tax and discontinued-operations disclosures.

nodes.title: PRODUCT DEVELOPMENTS
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s February 2022 pipeline update describes its research and development candidates, indications, and development phases. The text summarizes significant FDA, EU, and Japanese regulatory approvals, filings, and pending decisions from the prior year, covering COVID-19 vaccines and treatments, and products for cancer, inflammatory conditions, vaccines, and other diseases. It details collaboration partners and product-specific developments, including Comirnaty age and booster authorizations, Paxlovid use, Prevnar 20 recommendations, and a CRL for somatrogon. It also reports Xeljanz safety-label changes and an ongoing EU review of JAK inhibitors, notes Chinese approvals for Cresemba and Besponsa, and introduces late-stage programs for additional uses and new drug candidates.

nodes.title: PRODUCT/CANDIDATE
nodes.summary: The text lists Pfizer’s 2021 product candidates and proposed disease areas, including oncology, vaccines and infectious diseases, gene therapies, and other treatments, with collaboration and trademark notes. It reports that the Phase 3 JAVELIN Lung 100 trial of avelumab for first-line PD-L1-positive metastatic NSCLC missed overall- and progression-free-survival endpoints; its safety profile was consistent with prior studies, and results are forthcoming. It also says enrollment stopped in a placebo-controlled BNT162b2 pregnancy study because vaccination recommendations reduced enrollment, leaving insufficient sample size; FDA and EMA agreed. Further R&D information is referenced in the Form 10-K.

nodes.title: NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURE: ADJUSTED INCOME
key_items: Purchase Accounting Adjustments; Acquisition-Related Items; Discontinued Operations
nodes.summary: Explains Pfizer’s non-GAAP Adjusted income and Adjusted diluted EPS: definitions, purposes, use in evaluating and forecasting recurring operations, and role in employee incentives. Describes their limitations, lack of GAAP standardization, and relationship to comparable GAAP measures and other performance tools. Details exclusions for purchase accounting, acquisition costs, discontinued operations, and significant or volatile items, including the 2021 exclusion of pension remeasurement gains and losses. Provides 2019–2021 reconciliations of GAAP results to adjusted expenses, income, and diluted EPS, with notes explaining adjustment categories, examples, and tax rates.

nodes.title: ANALYSIS OF THE CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS
nodes.summary: The text reports continuing-operations cash flows for 2019–2021: operating cash provided was $32.9 billion in 2021, $10.5 billion in 2020, and $7.0 billion in 2019; investing and financing activities used cash in each year. It explains year-over-year drivers: operating changes reflect adjusted net income, acquisitions, pension contributions, timing of receipts and payments, Comirnaty-related deferred revenue and BioNTech accruals, and equity-related adjustments. Investing changes mainly reflect short-term investment purchases, redemptions, and the 2019 Array acquisition. Financing changes reflect short-term and long-term borrowing, debt issuance and repayments, dividends, and share repurchases. Discontinued-operation cash flows relate chiefly to Meridian, Upjohn, and the Mylan-Japan collaboration; 2020 financing inflows primarily came from long-term debt issuance.

nodes.title: ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION, LIQUIDITY, CAPITAL RESOURCES AND MARKET RISK
key_items: Off-Balance Sheet Arrangements, Contractual, and Other Obligations
nodes.summary: Pfizer says operating cash flow, financial assets, and access to credit and capital markets should meet foreseeable liquidity needs. It manages working capital conservatively, invests excess cash in liquid securities, and describes internal and external funding sources. The text covers a $1 billion sustainability-note offering, credit ratings, dividends and share repurchases, off-balance-sheet arrangements and major contractual obligations, and hyperinflationary operations. It outlines foreign-exchange, interest-rate, and equity-price risks, whose modeled adverse impacts were not significant, and says LIBOR transition should not materially affect liquidity or financial resources.

summary: Reviews Pfizer’s 2021 performance, business strategy, R&D, deals, operating environment, COVID-19 response and risks; critical accounting policies, estimates and contingencies; 2019–2021 revenue, expenses, taxes and operating results; pipeline candidates, regulatory developments and trial outcomes; and the definition, limitations and reconciliations of adjusted income and EPS. It analyzes operating, investing and financing cash flows, liquidity, capital resources, obligations, dividends, repurchases, funding and credit access, and foreign-exchange, interest-rate, equity-price and LIBOR-transition risks.

title: Accounting Standards and Market Risk
key_items: ITEM 7A. QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
summary: The page refers readers to Note 1B for recently adopted accounting standards and describes two standards not yet adopted: temporary optional relief for contracts and hedges tied to LIBOR or other discontinued rates, with elections available through December 31, 2022, and revised acquisition-date accounting for customer contract assets and liabilities, effective January 1, 2023, with early adoption permitted. The company expects neither standard to materially affect its consolidated financial statements. Market-risk disclosures are incorporated by reference to the relevant MD&A section.

title: ITEM 8. FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND SUPPLEMENTARY DATA

nodes.title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
key_items: Opinion on the Consolidated Financial Statements
Evaluation of the U.S. Medicare, Medicaid, and performance-based contract rebates accrual
Evaluation of gross unrecognized tax benefits
nodes.summary: The independent auditor gives an unqualified opinion that Pfizer’s 2021 and 2020 consolidated balance sheets and its three-year financial statements comply fairly with U.S. GAAP, and reports an unqualified opinion on internal financial controls. The report notes a 2021 change to immediately recognize pension and postretirement actuarial gains and losses. It describes management and auditor responsibilities, PCAOB-compliant audit procedures, and the role of critical audit matters. One matter is estimating U.S. Medicare, Medicaid, and performance-based rebate accruals, including controls, independent estimates, and comparison with historical payments. Another is evaluating uncertain tax positions; gross unrecognized tax benefits were $6.1 billion at year-end 2021.

nodes.title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
key_items: Evaluation of product and other product-related litigation; February 24, 2022
Evaluation of product and other product-related litigation
nodes.summary: The auditor identifies two critical audit matters: gross unrecognized tax benefits, assessed through controls testing, specialist review of tax-law interpretations and transfer pricing, inspection of tax settlements and limitation periods, and testing of uncertain-tax-position calculations; and product-related litigation, assessed through controls testing, review of counsel letters and Audit Committee minutes, comparison of historical estimates with resolved losses, and analysis of public company and industry information. The report notes litigation may cause substantial losses and involves uncertain judgments. The auditor’s service dates are unknown before at least 1942. Signed in New York on February 24, 2022.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statements of Income
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s consolidated income statement presents results for 2021, 2020, and 2019, in millions except per-share data. It lists revenues; operating costs and expenses, including cost of sales, selling and administrative, research and development, amortization, restructuring and acquisition-related costs, the Consumer Healthcare joint-venture gain, and other income or deductions; pretax income, taxes, continuing and discontinued operations, noncontrolling interests, and net income attributable to common shareholders. It also reports basic and diluted earnings per share by continuing and discontinued operations, weighted-average shares, and a note on the scope of expense figures.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income
nodes.summary: Pfizer Inc.’s consolidated statements of comprehensive income for 2021, 2020, and 2019 report net income; foreign currency translation, derivative, available-for-sale securities, and benefit-plan adjustments; other comprehensive income before and after tax; comprehensive income; amounts attributable to noncontrolling interests; and comprehensive income attributable to Pfizer. Notes identify where certain derivative and securities gains or losses were reclassified. Amounts are in millions.

nodes.title: Consolidated Balance Sheets
nodes.summary: Pfizer Inc. and subsidiaries’ consolidated balance sheets as of December 31, 2021 and 2020, in millions except per-share data. They itemize current and noncurrent assets, total assets, current and long-term liabilities, commitments and contingencies, and equity components—including preferred and common stock, additional paid-in capital, treasury stock, retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive loss, and noncontrolling interests—and report total liabilities and equity. The statements include share counts and debt and receivable allowance details, with accompanying notes referenced.

nodes.title: Consolidated Statements of Equity
nodes.summary: Pfizer Inc. and subsidiaries’ consolidated statements of equity for 2019–2021 show annual opening and closing balances and changes from net income, other comprehensive income or loss, declared common and preferred dividends, noncontrolling interests, share-based compensation, common-stock purchases, preferred-stock conversions and redemptions, the Upjohn Business distribution, and other items. The statement details preferred and common shares and stated value, additional paid-in capital, retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive loss, treasury stock, noncontrolling interests, and total equity; it references Notes 12 and 2B and accompanying notes.

nodes.title: Pfizer Inc.
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s consolidated statements of equity report changes from 2019–2021 in preferred and common stock, additional paid-in capital, retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive loss, treasury stock, noncontrolling interests, and total equity. Transactions include net income and other comprehensive loss, dividends, share-based payments, stock repurchases, preferred-stock conversions/redemptions, the Upjohn distribution, and other items. The consolidated cash flow statements for 2019–2021 detail operating, investing, and financing cash flows, including continuing and discontinued operations, noncash adjustments, investment activity, debt, repurchases, dividends, exchange-rate effects, and beginning and ending cash balances.

nodes.title: Pfizer Inc.
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s consolidated cash flow statements for 2021, 2020 and 2019 report operating, investing and financing cash flows, including continuing and discontinued operations, reconciliation adjustments, changes in assets and liabilities, and beginning-to-ending cash balances. Supplemental disclosures cover cash paid or received for taxes, interest and interest-rate hedges, plus noncash lease and Consumer Healthcare JV transactions. A note explains the JV gain, the investment and net assets exchanged, and cash conveyed.

nodes.title: Note 1. Basis of Presentation and Significant Accounting Policies
Basis of Presentation and 2021 Accounting Standard
key_items: B. New Accounting Standard Adopted in 2021
nodes.summary: Pfizer’s consolidated statements follow U.S. GAAP, include its parent and controlled subsidiaries, align international and U.S. subsidiary reporting periods, and eliminate significant intercompany transactions. The text describes the 2021 operating-segment reorganization and the treatment of Meridian, Upjohn, and the Mylan-Japan collaboration as discontinued operations or distributions, along with prior-period reclassifications, business-development impacts, and rounding conventions. Pfizer adopted an income-tax accounting standard in 2021 covering intraperiod and interim taxes, deferred taxes, franchise taxes, tax-law changes, and goodwill tax-basis step-ups; adoption had no material impact.

nodes.title: C. Change in Accounting Principle
nodes.summary: Pfizer adopted MTM accounting in Q1 2021, retrospectively applying immediate recognition of pension and postretirement actuarial gains and losses in other income/deductions, instead of deferring and amortizing them. The change reduced January 1, 2019 retained earnings by $6.0 billion, offset in accumulated other comprehensive loss, and was justified by improved transparency, fair-value alignment, and responsiveness to economic conditions. Tables reconcile its effects on 2019–2021 income, earnings per share, comprehensive income, cash flows, and balance-sheet items, including taxes, benefit obligations, retained earnings, and accumulated other comprehensive loss.

nodes.title: Estimates, Acquisitions, and Fair Value
nodes.summary: Pfizer explains how estimates and assumptions affect financial statements, are reviewed and adjusted, and may differ from actual outcomes amid business and regulatory risks. Acquisitions use the acquisition method, including fair-value recognition, goodwill or IPR&D treatment, expensing transaction costs, and remeasurement of contingent consideration. Fair value uses an exit-price approach, income, market, or cost valuation methods, and Level 1–3 inputs. The company describes techniques for valuing financial instruments and its review of third-party pricing.

nodes.title: G. Foreign Currency Translation
nodes.summary: Pfizer generally uses local currencies as functional currencies for international operations. It translates assets and liabilities at balance-sheet-date rates and income and expenses at period-average rates, recording resulting U.S. dollar translation effects in other comprehensive income or loss. Gains and losses from converting non-functional-currency monetary items are recorded in other income or deductions, net. In highly inflationary economies, monetary items use balance-sheet-date rates and adjustments go to other income or deductions, net, while non-monetary items use historical rates.

nodes.title: H. Revenues and Trade Accounts Receivable
key_items: Revenue Recognition; Our Sales Contracts; Deductions from Revenues
nodes.summary: Explains revenue recognition on product sales, short-term credit contracts, and estimates for returns, rebates, chargebacks, discounts, and sales incentives, including U.S. and international practices and related accrual balances. Describes customer and vaccine sales channels, concentration of revenue in major products, and the effect of patent expiry and generic competition. Outlines trade-receivable credit-loss estimation, monitoring, and write-offs; accounting for collaboration revenues, costs, royalties, reimbursements, and milestone payments; inventory valuation and impairment; and selling, informational, and administrative expense treatment, including advertising costs.

nodes.title: Revenue, Collaboration, Inventory and Expense Policies
key_items: J. Cost of Sales and Inventories
K. Selling, Informational and Administrative Expenses
nodes.summary: The page reports sales-related accruals for 2021 and 2020, excludes customer-collected taxes from revenue, and explains how trade receivables are valued and credit-loss allowances estimated, monitored, and written off. It describes accounting for collaboration revenues, costs, royalties, reimbursements, and milestone payments. Inventories are measured at the lower of cost or net realizable value using average actual cost, with impairment reviews. Selling, informational, and administrative costs are expensed as incurred; advertising expense totals and the timing of advertising-cost recognition are provided.

nodes.title: R&D, Long-Lived Assets, and Restructuring Policies
key_items: M. Amortization of Intangible Assets, Depreciation and Certain Long-Lived Assets
N. Restructuring Charges and Other Costs Associated with Acquisitions and Cost-Reduction/Productivity Initiatives
nodes.summary: Pfizer expenses R&D and pre-approval licensing payments when incurred or milestones are achieved; approved-product milestones are capitalized and generally amortized. The page explains capitalization, depreciation, amortization, expense classification, and impairment testing for property, intangible assets, and goodwill. It also describes acquisition-related and productivity restructuring costs, their accounting—including employee termination and transaction costs—and the business functions affected.

nodes.title: O. Cash Equivalents and Statement of Cash Flows
nodes.summary: Cash equivalents include highly liquid instruments such as certificates of deposit and time deposits with original maturities of three months or less; when held within a larger investment pool, qualifying items are classified as short-term investments. Cash-flow classification for fair-value or cash-flow hedges depends on the hedged items; net-investment hedge flows follow the hedging instrument’s nature, while flows from instruments not qualifying for hedge accounting follow their purpose and accounting nature.

nodes.title: P. Investments and Derivative Financial Instruments
nodes.summary: Investment classification depends on investment type, intent and ability to hold, and degree of influence. Public equities and available-for-sale debt are at fair value, with changes recognized in earnings or other comprehensive income, respectively; held-to-maturity debt is at amortized cost. Certain private equities use a measurement alternative based on cost, impairment, and observable price changes; significant-influence investments use equity accounting, including allocating acquisition cost excess to assets, liabilities, and goodwill. Realized sale gains and losses use specific identification. Financial assets are regularly assessed for impairment, with charges establishing a new cost basis. Derivatives are measured at fair value, with changes recorded in net income or, for qualifying hedges, other comprehensive income.

nodes.title: Q. Tax Assets and Liabilities and Income Tax Contingencies
nodes.summary: The text describes Pfizer’s accounting policies for current and deferred tax assets and liabilities, GILTI, cross-jurisdiction tax benefits, uncertain tax positions, and income-tax contingencies, including recognition, measurement, classification, and estimation uncertainty. It summarizes defined benefit, defined contribution, and postretirement plans and their actuarial measurement and expense treatment; accruals for legal and environmental contingencies and insurance recoveries; and fair-value accounting for share-based compensation. It also details the 2021 Trillium acquisition, accounted for as an asset acquisition with an R&D charge, and the 2019 Array acquisition, including consideration, employee compensation, and financing.

nodes.title: Tax, Benefit Plans, Contingencies, and Share-Based Payments
key_items: R. Pension and Postretirement Benefit Plans
nodes.summary: The notes explain how Pfizer recognizes uncertain tax benefits, classifies related liabilities, records interest and penalties, and assesses estimation uncertainty. They describe pension and postretirement plans, actuarial assumptions, plan asset measurement, and benefit-cost recognition. Legal and environmental contingencies include litigation, claims, investigations, guarantees, and indemnifications; losses are accrued when probable and estimable, with insurance recoveries recorded when assured. Share-based awards are generally measured at fair value and expensed over vesting periods.

Covers Pfizer’s U.S. GAAP consolidated reporting, segment and discontinued-operation changes, reclassifications, and adoption of an income-tax standard; the retrospective 2021 change to mark-to-market pension accounting and its financial-statement effects; estimates, acquisitions, and fair-value methods; foreign-currency translation; revenue recognition, sales deductions, receivables, collaborations, inventories, and advertising and other expenses; R&D, long-lived-asset impairment, and restructuring; cash and cash-flow classifications; investments, impairment, and derivatives; income taxes and contingencies; pension and postretirement plans; share-based compensation; and the Trillium and Array acquisitions.

nodes.title: Note 2. Acquisitions, Divestitures, Equity-Method Investments, Licensing Arrangements and Collaborative Arrangements
A. Acquisitions
nodes.summary: The note details three acquisitions. Pfizer acquired Trillium in 2021 for $2.0 billion net of cash, making it wholly owned; treated the deal as an asset acquisition and expensed $2.1 billion for acquired IPR&D, while recording acquired assets and assumed liabilities. Array was acquired in 2019 for $11.2 billion, with employee stock-option compensation expensed; its cancer portfolio and acquired intangible assets, goodwill, deferred taxes and debt are described, along with 2020 measurement-period adjustments. Therachon was acquired in 2019 for $322 million of consideration, plus potential milestones, and treated as an asset acquisition with a $337 million R&D charge.

nodes.title: B. Divestitures
nodes.summary: Pfizer reports selling Meridian on December 31, 2021, for about $51 million cash and recording a $167 million after-tax loss; transition services and a three-year manufacturing agreement followed, with no 2021 amounts recorded. It describes the 2020 all-stock Reverse Morris Trust separation of Upjohn and combination with Mylan to form Viatris, including ownership, the $12 billion payment to Pfizer, related debt financing and repayment of Pfizer debt, tax treatment, transferred net assets and equity adjustments, separation costs, and post-transaction agreements, balances, cash flows, and obligations. The text also presents discontinued-operations results and assets/liabilities held for sale by year, explaining their components, including Meridian litigation and sale loss, Upjohn debt interest and remeasurement, and other legacy-business adjustments.

nodes.title: C. Equity-Method Investments
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes its 2019 GSK Consumer Healthcare joint venture: Pfizer received a 32% stake, deconsolidated the business, and recorded an $8.1 billion pretax gain; it explains valuation assumptions, equity-method accounting, foreign-currency effects, dividends, earnings recognition lag, initial basis difference and its allocation and amortization, and 2019 segment income. It presents the JV’s summarized balance-sheet and operating results. Pfizer also explains its 11.7% ViiV stake, suspension of equity-method accounting after its carrying value fell to zero, subsequent dividend income, and provides headings for ViiV summarized financial information.

nodes.title: D. Licensing Arrangements
nodes.summary: The text includes financial tables for licensing arrangements as of and for the years ended December 31, 2019–2021. Pfizer’s April 2020 agreement with Valneva covers co-development and commercialization of the six-serotype Lyme vaccine candidate VLA15. Valneva may receive up to $308 million, including a paid $130 million upfront payment, $35 million in development milestones, and $143 million in early commercialization milestones; it funds 30% of development costs in exchange for tiered royalties, while Pfizer leads late-stage development and controls commercialization. Pfizer’s 2019 worldwide exclusive license from Akcea for investigational AKCEA-ANGPTL3-LRx included a $250 million upfront payment. In January 2022, Pfizer and Ionis announced discontinuation of Pfizer-led development and return of the product rights to Ionis.

nodes.title: E. Collaborative Arrangements
nodes.summary: The notes describe Pfizer’s collaborative arrangements and terms, payments, equity stakes, cost/profit sharing, and reported collaboration revenues and expenses for Beam, Arvinas, Myovant, CStone, and BioNTech. They detail restructuring and acquisition-related programs, costs, and accruals; other income and deductions; income taxes, effective-rate reconciliation, deferred taxes, uncertain tax positions, audits, and tax effects in comprehensive income; accumulated other comprehensive loss; and financial instruments, investments, borrowings, debt issuances and retirements, fair-value measurements, foreign-exchange and interest-rate risks, hedging methods, balances, and gains and losses.

nodes.title: F. Credit Risk
nodes.summary: Pfizer monitors credit risk across customers, financial institutions and investments. Receivables are generally unsecured, with significant balances due from wholesalers and governments. Investments are investment-grade, short-duration and subject to counterparty limits, primarily involving sovereign debt. Derivatives use ISDA agreements with daily collateral exchange; year-end net payable and receivable fair values and related collateral are reported. The notes also provide 2021 and 2020 inventory components and explain inventory changes and noncurrent inventory recoverability; disclose BioNTech amounts in current liabilities; detail PP&E by asset type, useful life and geography; and introduce identifiable intangible assets and goodwill.

Covers Pfizer’s acquisitions of Trillium, Array and Therachon; the Meridian sale and Upjohn separation, including related financial effects and discontinued operations; GSK and ViiV equity-method investments; Valneva and Akcea licensing agreements; and collaborations with Beam, Arvinas, Myovant, CStone and BioNTech. It also addresses restructuring, taxes, accumulated other comprehensive loss, financial instruments, debt, fair values, foreign-exchange and interest-rate risks, hedging, credit risk, receivables, inventory, property and equipment, and intangible assets and goodwill.

summary: Presents the independent auditor’s unqualified opinions on Pfizer’s 2019–2021 financial statements and internal controls, audit responsibilities, and critical audit matters involving rebates, uncertain tax positions, and litigation. Includes income, comprehensive income, balance-sheet, equity, and cash-flow statements with related disclosures. Notes cover accounting policies and the effects of pension accounting changes; acquisitions, divestitures, discontinued operations, investments, licensing and collaborations; and restructuring, taxes, financial instruments, risk management, debt, receivables, inventory, property, intangibles, and goodwill.

title: As of December 31, 2021

nodes.title: As of December 31, 2021 (intro)
nodes.summary: Pfizer reports identifiable intangible assets at December 31, 2021 and 2020, showing gross carrying amounts and accumulated amortization for finite-lived developed technology rights, brands and licensing assets, and indefinite-lived brands, IPR&D and licensing assets. Changes primarily reflect $500 million of capitalized Comirnaty milestones, foreign-currency effects and amortization. The text describes the nature and key components of each asset category, IPR&D and licensing-asset accounting, approval, amortization and impairment risks. Finite-lived assets have weighted-average useful lives of about eight years (seven for developed technology); amortization expense was $3.7 billion in 2021, $3.4 billion in 2020 and $4.5 billion in 2019, with forecasts of $3.279 billion for 2022, $2.936 billion for 2023, $2.686 billion for 2024, $2.500 billion for 2025 and $2.449 billion for 2026.

nodes.title: B. Goodwill
nodes.summary: Reports goodwill balances: $48.181 billion at January 1, 2020, with 2020 additions and foreign-exchange effects bringing it to $49.556 billion; 2021 foreign-exchange effects resulted in $49.208 billion. No goodwill was reallocated after the 2021 commercial reorganization; additions mainly reflect Array acquisition measurement-period adjustments. Note 11 describes employee pension, defined-contribution and retiree medical plans, and retrospective adoption of immediate recognition of actuarial gains and losses. It presents 2019–2021 pension and postretirement benefit costs, credits and other comprehensive income changes, explains actuarial remeasurement drivers and cost classification, and lists actuarial assumptions and their annual review and discount-rate methods. U.S. healthcare cost-trend assumptions for 2021 and 2020 are also provided.

nodes.title: C. Obligations and Funded Status
nodes.summary: The note presents 2021 and 2020 changes in pension and postretirement benefit obligations and plan assets, ending funded status, balance-sheet amounts, accumulated other comprehensive loss components, and plans whose obligations exceed assets. It covers U.S. and international pension plans and postretirement plans, with figures in millions. Footnotes explain obligation measures for frozen U.S. plans and international/postretirement plans, actuarial-assumption effects, the Upjohn spin-off reference, and that Pfizer’s main U.S. qualified plan and many international plans were overfunded at year-end 2021.

nodes.title: D. Plan Assets
nodes.summary: The note details Pfizer’s 2020 and 2021 pension and postretirement plan assets by investment type, target allocation, fair-value hierarchy level, and NAV-measured amounts, including discontinued operations. It explains NAV reconciliation and categories such as government obligations, partnerships, and other investments, and provides a 2020–2021 Level 3 investment rollforward for international pension plans. It also describes valuation methods and assumptions for cash, equity, fixed income, and other investments; commingled-fund and partnership valuation; permitted derivatives; and the plans’ long-term investment objectives, allocation strategy, return expectations, and potential target adjustments.

nodes.title: E. Cash Flows
nodes.summary: The company funds qualified pension plans at least to the minimum required by employee-benefit and local tax laws. It provides expected 2022 employer contributions and projected benefit payments for 2022–2026 and 2027–2031 across U.S. and international pension and postretirement plans. The projections include benefits paid by the plans or from general assets and use current actuarial assumptions.

nodes.title: F. Defined Contribution Plans
F. Defined Contribution Plans (intro)
nodes.summary: Pfizer reports global defined-contribution plan charges of $732 million in 2021, $685 million in 2020 and $659 million in 2019; U.S. plans include employee contributions, employer matching and an annual non-contributory savings contribution. The text details share-repurchase authorizations, a completed $6.8 billion 2019 accelerated repurchase, annual purchase figures and $5.3 billion remaining authorization at year-end 2021. It also describes conversion and elimination of Series A preferred stock, the Common ESOP and its costs, and share-based award types, 2019 Plan limits, available shares and methods for meeting award obligations.

nodes.title: Equity, Share Repurchases, and Employee Stock Ownership
key_items: B. Preferred Stock and Employee Stock Ownership Plans
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes its board-authorized share repurchase programs, including a $6.8 billion 2019 accelerated share repurchase (163.5 million shares at an average $41.42 each), annual purchases and costs for 2019–2021, and $5.3 billion of authorization remaining at year-end 2021. It also reports conversion of all Series A preferred stock held by an ESOP trust into 1,070,369 common shares in May 2020 and its subsequent elimination. Since then, a Common ESOP has held shares allocated to U.S. defined contribution plan participants; compensation costs were $19 million in 2021 and 2020 and $20 million in 2019.

nodes.title: Note 13. Share-Based Payments
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes its share-based compensation programs, award types, eligibility, terms, vesting and performance conditions, valuation methods, expense recognition, and the 2019 Plan’s share limits and availability. The note also covers retirement-related TSRU conversions and historical PTSRUs; 2019–2021 award activity, compensation costs and tax benefits; valuation assumptions; and 2021 balances and activity for TSRUs, PTUs, RSUs, PPSs, PSAs, BPAs, and stock options, including grants, vesting, forfeitures, settlements, exercise prices, remaining terms, and intrinsic values.

nodes.title: Note 14. Earnings Per Common Share Attributable to Pfizer Inc. Common Shareholders
nodes.summary: Note 14 details Pfizer’s basic and diluted EPS calculations for 2019–2021, listing income attributable to common shareholders, preferred dividends, discontinued operations, assumed conversions, weighted-average basic and diluted shares, and common-share equivalents. It notes that certain outstanding equivalents were excluded as anti-dilutive. Common ESOP shares, including reinvested dividends, count as outstanding; allocated Preferred ESOP shares were assumed converted for diluted EPS until their conversion in May 2020.

nodes.title: Note 15. Leases
nodes.summary: Pfizer leases real estate, fleet and equipment for 1–30 years, with certain extension or termination options; some fleet leases have residual guarantees. Leases may include variable payments and non-lease charges; variable lease costs were $381 million in 2021, $380 million in 2020 and $326 million in 2019. Pfizer combines lease and non-lease components, assesses leases at inception, and measures operating-lease assets and liabilities using present value and estimated borrowing rates. The note reports balance-sheet classifications and balances, lease-cost components, lease terms and discount rates, cash flows and sale-leaseback results, and a maturity reconciliation of undiscounted payments to recorded liabilities.

nodes.title: Note 16. Contingencies and Certain Commitments
nodes.summary:
Note 16. Contingencies and Certain Commitments
We and certain of our subsidiaries are subject to numerous contingencies arising in the ordinary course of business, including tax and legal contingencies. The following outlines our legal contingencies. For a discussion of our tax contingencies, see Note 5B.

nodes.title: A. Legal Proceedings
nodes.summary: Pfizer describes legal contingencies including patent, product-liability, commercial, environmental, and government matters, their potential financial and criminal consequences, uncertainty, accrual practices, and inability to estimate losses beyond accruals. It explains its $1 million disclosure threshold for environmental sanctions and criteria for identifying principal matters. title: DESCRIPTION OF CAPITAL STOCK
key_items: Anti-takeover Effects of the Certificate of Incorporation, By-laws and Delaware Law
summary: Pfizer’s charter authorizes 12 billion common shares ($0.05 par) and 27 million no-par preferred shares. Common stock has one vote per share, no redemption, conversion, call, or preemptive rights; dividends are board-declared, and holders share ratably in liquidation assets. Outstanding shares are fully paid and nonassessable; they trade as PFE on the NYSE. The board sets preferred-stock series terms and share counts. Charter and bylaw provisions may impede control changes, including limits on special-meeting calls, board powers over preferred stock, rights, size and vacancies, and prohibiting written stockholder consent. Delaware DGCL Section 203 generally restricts business combinations with 15%-plus interested stockholders for three years, subject to specified board, ownership, or stockholder-approval exceptions; this may delay or deter takeovers and depress share value.

title: DESCRIPTION OF DEBT SECURITIES

nodes.title: Principal, Maturity and Interest
nodes.summary: The debt securities are governed by Pfizer’s 2001 base indenture, as amended by the ninth supplemental indenture dated March 6, 2017; the indentures, not this summary, define holders’ rights. The €1 billion 2022 notes and €750 million 2027 notes mature March 6 of their respective years, were issued in €100,000 denominations and €1,000 increments, and bear annual interest of 0.250% and 1.000%. Interest is paid each March 6 using ACTUAL/ACTUAL (ICMA), to holders of record on the preceding February 15. The Bank of New York Mellon, London Branch, is paying agent, subject to change on notice; payments flow through the agent to Euroclear and/or Clearstream.

nodes.title: Issuance in Euros
nodes.summary: Notes are payable in euros, including principal, any premium, interest, and additional amounts. If euros become unavailable due to exchange controls or other circumstances beyond the issuer’s control, or cease to be used by euro-adopting EMU members or for specified international banking transactions, payments will temporarily be made in U.S. dollars. The issuer will convert the euro amount using the latest available market rate, determined at its sole discretion. Such dollar payments are not defaults, and the trustee and paying agent have no duty to obtain rates, convert currencies, or handle redenominations.

nodes.title: Payment of Additional Amounts
nodes.summary: The text explains that Pfizer generally pays note amounts without U.S. tax withholding and grosses up payments to non-U.S. beneficial owners when withholding is legally required, subject to exceptions for specified U.S. connections or tax statuses, intermediary ownership, noncompliance with requested tax documentation, non-withholding taxes, certain taxes and paying-agent or timing circumstances, later legal changes, and FATCA. It defines “United States” and “United States person,” states the notes are unsecured, unsubordinated obligations ranking equally with similar Pfizer debt and are NYSE-listed without a continuing listing obligation, and describes indenture covenants restricting certain mergers or substantially-all asset transfers while imposing no other restrictive covenants or specified financial protections.

nodes.title: Tax Exceptions, Note Ranking and Listing

It defines “United States” and “United States person” for relevant provisions. Pfizer’s notes are unsecured, unsubordinated general obligations ranking equally with its other such debt, and are NYSE-listed, though Pfizer need not maintain the listing and may delist them.

nodes.title: Covenants
nodes.summary: The indenture restricts Pfizer from merging or transferring substantially all its assets, but permits transfers of less than substantially all. It otherwise lacks protective covenants, including protections for highly leveraged transactions and covenants on debt, coverage, repurchases, dividends, financial ratios, acquisitions, guarantees, liens, or sale-leasebacks. Pfizer may issue additional notes without holder consent on substantially identical terms, forming one series if U.S. tax-fungible; none may be issued during an event of default for that series.

nodes.title: Optional Redemption of 2022 Notes and 2027 Notes; Redemption for Tax Reasons; No Sinking Fund
nodes.summary: The issuer may redeem 2022 and 2027 notes before specified near-maturity dates at the greater of par or the present value of remaining payments discounted using the Comparable Government Bond Rate plus 15 basis points, plus accrued interest; on or after those dates, redemption is at par plus accrued interest. The text sets out interest-payment, day-count, notice, payment, and post-redemption accrual rules; defines the comparable German government bond, its rate, the Independent Investment Banker, and Reference Treasury Dealers; explains partial-redemption selection; and states that the notes have no sinking fund.

nodes.title: Redemption for Tax Reasons
nodes.summary: If a U.S. law, regulation, ruling, or official interpretation change announced or effective on or after February 28, 2017, causes or is expected—based on an opinion from independent, recognized tax counsel selected by the issuer—to cause additional tax-related payments on a note series, the issuer may redeem that entire series, but not part of it. It must give holders 10–60 days’ prior notice and pay 100% of principal plus accrued and unpaid interest, including additional amounts, through but excluding the redemption date.

Exchange of Global Notes for Certificated Notes

The text describes each clearing system’s services, governance, participants, and payment procedures; settlement, trading-day and time-zone limitations, and the systems’ ability to change procedures; and conditions for exchanging global notes for definitive certificates, including denominations and payment, transfer, and tax-charge arrangements.

nodes.title: Modification of Indenture
nodes.summary: A supplemental indenture may generally modify noteholders’ rights with consent from holders of a majority in principal amount of all affected outstanding series voting as one class. However, changes to maturity, principal or interest payments, payment currency, enforcement rights, conversion rights, specified consent or waiver thresholds, or provisions governing waivers of past defaults or certain covenants require each affected holder’s consent.

nodes.title: Events of Default
nodes.summary: Events of default include missed principal or premium payments, sinking fund or interest payments overdue by 60 days, uncured covenant breaches after 90 days’ written notice, and specified bankruptcy or insolvency actions. Defaults are generally series-specific; other-debt defaults do not count, and the trustee may withhold notice except for payment defaults. The trustee or holders of at least 33% of a series may accelerate its debt; a majority may rescind acceleration under stated payment, cure, and timing conditions. A majority of affected series may waive defaults, except payment defaults and provisions requiring each holder’s consent. Trustee action may require reasonable indemnity, and majority holders may direct proceedings subject to limits. The issuer must provide an annual certificate reporting indenture compliance and any defaults.

nodes.title: Defeasance
nodes.summary: Defeasance means discharge from some or all indenture obligations. Subject to additional conditions, depositing sufficient cash or government securities irrevocably with the trustee to cover a series’ principal, interest, premiums, and other sums through maturity or redemption allows the issuer to choose full discharge for that series or release from specified restrictive covenants and certain events of default. The issuer must provide the trustee an officer’s certificate and counsel’s opinion confirming all defeasance conditions have been met.
